To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we identified three HLB‐B53‐restricteed epitopes in HIV-1 gag p24, one of which showed no cross-reactivity to other HIV-1 clades, and that we re-defined the peptide-binding motif for HLB-B53 to include other P-2 anchors.
we used a novel approach to identify CTL responses in a cohort of clade‐A HIV‐1 infected individuals.
we identified three novel HLA‐B*53‐restricted CTL epitopes in the HIV‐1 gag protein.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel immunological tools to aid the design of vaccines against human immunodeficiency viruses (HIVs).
understanding the immune responses to HIV‐1 in African populations.
understanding the mechanisms by which the immune system responds to HIV infection and with using this knowledge to design effective vaccines against HIV.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the HLA‐B*53 allele is a major determinant of HIV‐1‐specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTL) responses in African individuals, and that the CTL responses in African individuals are directed against multiple clade A epitopes in the HIV‐1 GAG protein.

HLA‐B*53 is the only HLA allele that is associated with a reduced risk of HIV‐1 disease progression, and this association is due to the presence of a particular amino acid at position 2 in the HLA‐B binding groove.
the HIV‐1 vaccine should contain all the epitopes that are recognized by CTLs in the infected individual.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we identified 3 novel HLA‐B*53 restricted epitopes in HIV-1 gag p24 in clade A infected Gambians.
we have defined a number of novel HLA‐B*53‐restricted epitope peptides in HIV‐1 clade A gag p24, which would not have been identified using the HLA‐B35 motif.
we have defined three new HLA‐B*53‐restricted HIV‐1 gag epitopes, which are not cross‐reactive to other HIV‐ 1 clades, and which are likely to be important in controlling HIV‐1 infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the HLA‐B allele, B53, which is common in Africa, is capable of presenting a variety of peptides from the Gag protein of HIV‐1.
CTL epitopes in HIV-1 gag are clade-specific, and the epitopes are not predicted from the peptide-binding motif.
we can use structural analysis of the HLA molecule to define the peptide‐binding motifs of HLA molecules and that these motifs can be used to identify potential CTL epitopes in the HIV‐1 genome.
